clue.text: Fleet holding one ringleader for crime at sea

indicators.note: a word that is holding something has it gripped inside its own letters

parts.note: fleet means quick, as does pacy
the Roman numeral for one
the leader of ring is its first letter; the word splits as ring plus leader

explanation.surface: A navy squadron harbouring the chief instigator of a maritime offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' looks like a navy, but here it is the adjective for speedy. One and the ring's leader go inside it together.
explanation.definitionFit: Piracy is robbery or violence committed on the high seas, the classic offence of the maritime world.

clue.text: Conceited person's report covered by flier

indicators.note: by means beside, so the bird's name is placed straight after what comes before

parts.note: a pop is the report of a gun or cork
in, as in wrapped in a coat, means covered
a jay is a bird of the crow family

explanation.surface: A vain individual's bulletin is overshadowed by an airborne rival.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A popinjay is a vain, foppish person who chatters about himself; the word originally meant a parrot.

clue.text: Right conclusion producing tears

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for right
a conclusion is an ending

explanation.surface: A proper finish to a story that leaves the audience weeping.
explanation.walkthrough: The tears are rips, not crying: the word rhymes with 'bears', not 'beers'.
explanation.definitionFit: To rend is to rip apart, so rending is the act of making rips in cloth or flesh.

clue.text: No thoroughbred in unusually short race

indicators.note: something done unusually is done out of the normal order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A horse of humble breeding taking part in a sprint, oddly enough.
explanation.definitionFit: A cart-horse is a heavy draught animal, the very opposite of a sleek racing thoroughbred.

clue.text: One seeking satisfaction with second helping

definitions.text: One seeking satisfaction with second helping

parts.words: One seeking satisfaction with second helping
parts.note: surface reading: a hungry diner wanting a second portion to fill up
setter's reading: demanding 'satisfaction' for an insult, assisted by a second, the friend who arranges a formal fight with pistols or swords

explanation.surface: A greedy eater who will only be content after another plateful.
explanation.walkthrough: To demand satisfaction was to challenge someone to a formal fight; each party had a second to arrange it.
explanation.definitionFit: A duellist is a combatant in a formal duel, traditionally fought to obtain satisfaction for an insult with seconds in attendance.

clue.text: Plant holding up broken units as not good enough

indicators.note: in a down entry, a word holding up another sits beneath it and supports it from below
something broken is smashed apart, so these letters are put back together in a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
a plant is an industrial works or factory

explanation.surface: A factory propping up defective units that fail to meet the standard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' tempts a gardener's reading, but it is an industrial works; in this down entry it sits underneath the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsatisfactory means falling short of what is acceptable or required.

clue.text: Like numbers perhaps for members, not general bar

definitions.text: Like numbers perhaps for members, not general
definitions.meaning: first meaning: describing an anaesthetic (a thing that numbs) applied to limbs rather than putting the whole patient under

explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' are things that numb, not figures, and 'members' are limbs; the opposite of a general anaesthetic is the answer. In Britain, your pub nearby is called this.
explanation.definitionFit: A local anaesthetic numbs one part of the body, and the local is a British name for the pub nearest one's home.

clue.text: Language coming from capital I analysed

indicators.note: letters coming from a phrase emerge out of it, running unbroken across the word gaps

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: A tongue that emerges when the capital letter I is subjected to analysis.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside capITAL I ANalysed; 'capital' suggests Rome, which fits the scene nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian is the Romance tongue spoken in Italy and parts of Switzerland.

clue.text: Make an effort, securing objective with it

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast inside, so one word grips the other

parts.note: to try is to make an effort
an objective is an end or aim

explanation.surface: Advice to work hard while keeping your goal firmly in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With it' looks like part of the instruction, but it is the definition: the slang for fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: To be 'with it' is to be fashionable and up to date, which is what trendy describes.

clue.text: Restrain doctor attending flier — that may be required by air traffic control

definitions.text: that may be required by air traffic control

parts.note: to restrain is to hold in
a GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor
attending an event is being at it
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: Holding back a medic who is tending a bird, as instructed by the control tower.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description rather than a synonym: the whole answer is something a controller might demand.
explanation.definitionFit: A holding pattern is the oval circuit aircraft fly while waiting for clearance to land, as directed by controllers.

clue.text: Short of brass, alternatively use up iron

indicators.note: doing it alternatively means arranging things another way, so these letters take a different order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Out of copper alloy, so a metalworker consumes iron instead.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass is British slang for money, though the metal theme of 'iron' disguises that.
explanation.definitionFit: Penurious means extremely poor, and to be short of brass is to lack money.

clue.text: Constant speed in rickety aircraft

parts.note: c is the symbol for the speed of light, a physical constant
speed is a rate of travel

explanation.surface: A steady velocity maintained in a shaky old plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' joins the wordplay to the definition, and does not mean one thing goes inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Crate is slang for a decrepit old vehicle, especially a battered aeroplane.

clue.text: Heeding changes, sounded like members of team?

indicators.note: a word that changes takes on a new form, here by reordering its letters

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Taking notice of alterations, as players in a side might.
explanation.walkthrough: The team is a team of horses pulling a carriage, not a sports side; the question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A team can be horses harnessed together, and the noise a horse makes is a neigh.

clue.text: Counted — bound to include everyone

indicators.note: to include something is to take it within, so one word goes inside another

parts.note: bound with rope is tied
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A tally certain to take in the whole population.
explanation.definitionFit: To tally is to count up or reckon a total, so tallied is a past tense of counting.

clue.text: Exchange rate, partly, as subject for management course?

indicators.note: only partly present means just a portion of the words is used, read straight through

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Currency values studied as a topic on a business school programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside exchANGE Rate. The management course is not a business one but the kind aimed at people with a temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Anger management courses teach people to control their temper, so rage is their subject.

clue.text: Catch fish, including first of salmon, as early bird

indicators.note: including something means taking it inside, so the capture word wraps round the kept letter

parts.note: to net is to catch

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: the opening letter of salmon
a ling is a long food fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: An angler landing fish, salmon among them, at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early bird' suggests a dawn riser, but it means a bird at an early stage of life. The kept letter goes inside the catch word, then the fish follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A nestling is a young bird not yet old enough to leave the nest, so a bird early in life.

clue.text: Do what MPs do, as support is overdue

parts.note: a leg supports a table or chair
taken as written
overdue means late

explanation.surface: Behaving like a member of parliament, since backing has not arrived on time.
explanation.walkthrough: MPs are Members of Parliament, the UK's elected lawmakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament's main job is to make laws, which is what to legislate means.

clue.text: Killer charged in Spain

parts.note: surface reading: a murderer formally accused by the Spanish courts
setter's reading: one who is charged by a bull in the ring, and who kills it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged' reads as a legal accusation; it is the bull's rush at its opponent in the bullring.
explanation.definitionFit: A toreador is a bullfighter, a figure of the Spanish arena where bulls charge and are killed.

clue.text: Climber quietly tucked into second small meal

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
wee is Scottish for small

indicators.note: something tucked into another is pushed inside it

parts.note: tea is an afternoon or evening meal
p, piano, is the musical direction to play quietly

explanation.surface: A mountaineer slipping silently into a second light lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' suggests a mountaineer but is a climbing plant. 'Second small meal' looks like a single phrase; it splits into three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet pea is a fragrant garden plant that climbs by tendrils up canes or trellises.

clue.text: Racing dog beat favourite

parts.note: to whip is to beat
the teacher's pet is the favourite

explanation.surface: A greyhound that outran the bookmakers' top choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Favourite' and 'beat' play on racing language, but they are a lash and a darling.
explanation.definitionFit: A whippet is a slender, fast breed of dog, like a small greyhound, raced in northern England.

clue.text: How American in the ranks operates gadget

parts.note: a GI is an American private soldier; the possessive adds S
MO, modus operandi, is the way someone operates
surface padding that frames the phrase 'how ... operates', the meaning of the following block

explanation.surface: Describing the method a US soldier uses to work a device.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as 'a GI's MO': MO, modus operandi, is the way someone operates, so 'How' and 'operates' together give it.
explanation.definitionFit: Gismo, also spelt gizmo, is informal for a clever little device or gadget.

clue.text: Flag need in some quarters

indicators.note: in places one word within the other

parts.note: south, east and north are three of the four compass points, or quarters
a need is a lack

explanation.surface: A banner is required in certain districts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' looks like a noun, a banner, but it is the verb meaning to tire. Quarters are compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to lose energy or slow down, which is what slacken means.

clue.text: Help make fit for sport

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to press something tight so it will go into a space
second meaning: a racket game played in a walled court

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a personal trainer getting someone fit; 'fit' here means to go into a space.
explanation.definitionFit: To squash is to squeeze something so it fits into a space, and squash is also a racket sport played against walls.

clue.text: Piano introducing new theme initially in piece of music

indicators.note: introducing something means putting it in, so the outer word takes the others inside

parts.note: piano is the musical term for soft or quiet
N is the abbreviation for new

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of theme

explanation.surface: A pianist bringing in a fresh motif at the start of a composition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piano' looks like the instrument but is the dynamic marking for soft playing.
explanation.definitionFit: A quintet is a composition written for five performers, so a piece of music.

clue.text: Tribute directed towards John, Paul, or George, say

parts.note: to means towards
each is a saint, so a saint: A plus ST

explanation.surface: A homage aimed at three of the Beatles.
explanation.walkthrough: The names suggest the Beatles, but each is also a saint: St John, St Paul, St George.
explanation.definitionFit: A toast is a tribute paid by raising glasses and drinking to someone's honour.

clue.text: Critically examine oddly deficient parties with a will

parts.note: to test is to examine critically

indicators.note: lacking the odd-numbered letters means only the even ones remain

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of parties

explanation.surface: Scrutinise strangely lacking celebrations, done with determination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With a will' suggests eagerness, but it is the legal sense: having made a will.
explanation.definitionFit: Testate is the legal term for someone who has died having left a valid will.

clue.text: Leader of Athens in final phase

indicators.note: in says the answer is sitting inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A Greek chief in the last stage of a campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside finAL PHAse; the leader is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, not a politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, the one that heads the list in Athens.

clue.text: Set aside each religious book penned by cardinal

parts.note: ea is the abbreviation for each

indicators.note: penned by means shut in by, as in a pen, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: cardinal red is a deep scarlet
Mark is one of the Gospels of the New Testament

explanation.surface: Every holy text written by a senior churchman is put on one side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penned' suggests writing, but it means enclosed; the cardinal is the colour of his robes.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark is to reserve or set aside funds or items for a particular purpose.

clue.text: Derby supporter in US — and that's strange

indicators.note: strange means odd or out of the ordinary, so these letters are put in an unusual order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fan of an English horse race in America finds it peculiar.
explanation.walkthrough: In America a derby is a bowler hat, not a horse race or a local football match.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatstand is a pole with hooks on which hats, such as a derby, are hung and held up.

clue.text: Singer vocalised second lowest note for us

indicators.note: something vocalised is spoken out, so it is the sound that counts, not the spelling

parts.note: a tenor is a male singing voice

explanation.surface: A vocalist sang the second-lowest note of the scale for the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The note is a banknote, not a musical one: in Britain the ten-pound note is the second smallest after the fiver.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenner is a ten-pound note, the second lowest denomination of banknote in British currency.
